messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Vignette:
Arjun Patel was 26 when he came to treatment, a married South Asian American man working as an editor for a small digital publishing company. He described the traumatic event in a halting, carefully controlled way, as if speaking too directly might pull him back into it. Several months earlier, he had been stopped by police late at night while walking home after staying late at the office. He remembered the cold with unusual clarity first: the air had turned sharp after sunset, and when one of the officers pushed him against the hood of the patrol car, the metal shocked through his shirt and into his skin. His cheek was pressed to the surface, one arm pinned awkwardly behind him, his body twisted in a way that had left him struggling not to panic. He could smell the mix of car exhaust, damp pavement, and the officer’s clothing at such close range. What stayed with him most, though, was not only fear. It was the helpless humiliation of it, and then the grief that seemed to open inside him afterward, as if something in the world he had trusted had been permanently broken.

In the days after, Arjun tried to return to work and to life with his wife as if the event were over because it had ended. Instead, he found that the experience returned in fragments that felt immediate and physical. If the air from an office vent hit his forearms with a certain chill, or if he stepped outside into a temperature that matched that night, his body seemed to recognize it before his mind did. He would stiffen, his shoulders drawing up, and sometimes he felt his torso subtly turning as though bracing again against the hood of the car. When memories came, they were not only pictures. He said there were moments when he could smell it all again—the cold air, the street, the exhaust—and those moments unnerved him because they made the past feel less like a memory and more like something still happening.

He also became frightened by changes inside himself. At times, especially when a memory started to surface, he would begin to feel detached, unreal, as though he were no longer fully inside his surroundings. That sensation itself became one of the things he dreaded most. The beginning of that floaty, distant feeling seemed to signal danger. He would stop what he was doing, grip the edge of a desk or countertop, and wait for it to pass, worried that if he let it deepen he would lose control completely.

Certain situations became charged in ways that embarrassed him and were hard to explain. Being alone with women was especially difficult. During the stop, a female officer had been nearby while he was pinned and searched, and now even ordinary workplace situations carried a sense of exposure and alarm. As an editor, he often had one-on-one meetings with writers, many of them women, to go over drafts. He began leaving the conference room door open, scheduling calls instead of in-person meetings, or asking colleagues to sit in “just for a minute” under transparent work-related pretexts. He knew these maneuvers looked odd. He felt ashamed of them, and ashamed that his mind treated ordinary encounters as if they were unsafe. Over time his work narrowed; he became less available, less spontaneous, and more dependent on controlling the setting.

At home, his wife noticed that he had grown distant and heavy with sadness. When he talked about the event at all, what came through was grief rather than anger. Remembering it seemed to break something open in him. He would go quiet, eyes lowered, as if mourning not only what happened but the person he had been before. He had come to believe that his reactions proved something bad about him. A stronger person, he was certain, would have put it behind him. Instead, he watched himself flinch at cold air, reorganize meetings, and brace when he felt unreal, and concluded that he was “a lousy coper.” That judgment had spread outward into the rest of his life. Work that had once mattered to him now felt flat and pointless. Even time with his wife no longer carried the same sense of future. He found himself thinking that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, and beyond that, that nothing good could happen to him again.

By the time he sought help, these beliefs had settled into his daily life with a bleak certainty. What finally brought him in was a recent incident at work when the office air conditioning kicked on during a meeting with a female colleague. The cold touched his skin, he caught himself starting to drift into that unreal feeling, and his body pulled tight into the same twisted posture before he abruptly ended the meeting and left. He was shaken not only by the episode but by what it seemed to confirm to him—that he was no longer someone who could trust himself in ordinary situations. In coming to therapy, Arjun said he wanted relief, but even more than that he wanted to know whether any part of his life could feel meaningful again. What frightened him most was the possibility that the night with the police had already decided the rest of his future.
